# Introduction

Urban transport planners increasingly rely on open-source tools to estimate pedestrian, cycle and motor traffic flows on street networks. The tools benchmarked here — cityseer [@simons2022cityseer], madina [@sevtsuk2025madina], sDNA [@cooper2020sdna], flownet [@krantz2024flownet] and aequilibrae [@aequilibrae2024] — span very different modelling traditions: network centrality and space syntax, gravity and floating-catchment-area demand models, path-sized logit assignment and user-equilibrium traffic assignment. Yet no systematic benchmark has compared these tools against the same observed counts, on the same networks, with the same demand inputs, so evidence-based tool choice remains difficult.

A structural gap motivates this work: most tools belong to the all-or-nothing (AoN) shortest-path family, which assigns each origin–destination pair to a single deterministic route. Only a few implement dispersed or multi-path assignment, spreading flow across several plausible routes via stochastic user equilibrium (SUE), user equilibrium (UE) or path-sized logit (PSL) models. Whether the route-choice model class materially affects predictive performance against real counts is untested, because tools are rarely run side-by-side on common ground-truth data.

This paper addresses three research questions:

1. **Does the route-choice model class matter?** Do dispersed and equilibrium assignment models (UE, PSL, dispersion-tolerant OD betweenness) predict observed flows better than the AoN shortest-path baseline?
2. **Does demand realism dominate algorithm sophistication?** Does a real census-derived origin–destination matrix outperform a synthetic gravity model, and does the choice of demand input swamp the choice of assignment algorithm?
3. **Does a composite efficiency score change the rankings?** Runtime and memory requirements vary by orders of magnitude across tools, so any honest comparison must reward accuracy per unit of computational resource — and doing so may reorder the tools relative to an accuracy-only ranking.

The benchmark presented here answers these questions with a reproducible suite (DVC pipeline, Docker image, pinned versions) and a single composite metric, the *efficiency score* (Equation @eq-efficiency). Results are organised by mode — walking (Leuven), driving (Leeds) and cycling (a coverage gap) — and all tables and figures are computed live from the benchmark result files at render time.

# Methods

## Benchmark suite design

Results were produced by a reproducible benchmark suite, defined as a DVC pipeline (`dvc.yaml`) with a `Dockerfile` for containerised reproduction (`dvc repro` regenerates all stages, and `dvc.lock` pins the state of every stage). Each tool is run by a dedicated script in `scripts/` (`bench_centrality.py`, `bench_cityseer_od.py`, `bench_sdna.py`, `bench_flownet.py`, `bench_aequilibrae.py`, and the demand-experiment runners `run_cityseer_demand_experiments.py` and `run_madina_demand_experiments.py`), driven by shared configuration (`config/cities.yaml`) and shared metrics helpers (`scripts/utils/`). Per-tool results are merged into per-city result tables (`results/leuven_results.csv`, `results/leeds_results.csv`), which all tables and figures in this paper read directly during rendering.

## Tools

Eight tool configurations are compared: **cityseer** (network centrality), **cityseer_demand** (cityseer's gravity demand model), **cityseer_od** (OD betweenness with configurable dispersion and tolerance), **madina** (topological betweenness and weighted betweenness), **madina_worldpop** (floating-catchment-area gravity with WorldPop demand), **sDNA+** (hybrid centrality), **flownet** (path-sized logit assignment) and **aequilibrae** (all-or-nothing and user-equilibrium assignment).

## Ground truth and demand

Ground truth comprises Leuven Telraam pedestrian counts (walk mode) [@telraam2024] and Leeds Department for Transport annual average daily traffic (AADT) counts (drive mode) [@dft2023aadt]. Demand inputs differ by design: Leeds demand-driven tools are fed a real 2011 Census journey-to-work origin–destination matrix (`pct::get_od`, MSOA level; used by cityseer_od and aequilibrae), whereas a synthetic gravity demand (WorldPop residential origins × OSM-POI attractors) is used for the gravity-family tools (cityseer_demand, madina_worldpop) and for flownet, and for the Leuven OD runs. Comparing cityseer_od (real OD) with madina_worldpop (synthetic gravity) on the same Leeds network therefore isolates the effect of demand realism on otherwise comparable assignment frameworks.

## Metrics and the efficiency score

Predictive performance is measured with R² against observed counts alongside runtime (`compute_time_s`), peak memory (`peak_memory_mb`) and throughput (`segments_per_sec`). Two R² variants are in use: linear R² (`compute_metrics`) for the centrality and gravity tools, and log-log R² (`compute_metrics_loglog`) for cityseer_od and aequilibrae, whose flows span orders of magnitude. **R² values from the two variants are not directly comparable** — a point we return to in Limitations. Sample sizes are small: 22 matched Telraam sensors in Leuven and 181–197 matched AADT links in Leeds (where recorded).

To combine accuracy with computational cost we use the composite efficiency score:

$$ \mathrm{efficiency\_score} = \frac{\max(R^2, 0)}{\log_{10}(1 + t) \cdot \log_{10}(1 + m)} $$ {#eq-efficiency}

where $t$ is runtime in seconds and $m$ is peak memory in MB (@eq-efficiency). Code complexity is quantified as lines of code (LoC, non-blank, non-comment) of each tool's integration script plus its source code.

Leeds is modelled within a 10 km buffer clip around central Leeds (235.7k / 233.2k / 63.9k walk/cycle/drive edges), which introduces a boundary artefact for zone-based dispersion (see Limitations).

## Tool complexity

Table @tbl-complexity quantifies integration effort and codebase size per tool. The integration LoC column counts the benchmark scripts that wrap each tool; the source LoC column counts the tool's own code, excluding native cores where the tool is a Python binding (cityseer's Rust core and aequilibrae's C++ core are deliberately excluded).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-complexity
#| tbl-cap: "Code complexity by tool: integration script LoC, tool source LoC and total (non-blank, non-comment lines). cityseer and aequilibrae totals exclude native (Rust/C++) cores."
import pandas as pd

# Verified LoC counts from the benchmark runs (paper outline, 2026-08-07): integration scripts per
# tool (cityseer 194+913+329, flownet 180+133) and tool source (flownet is R, deparsed, 34 functions;
# sDNA+ is C++).
tbl_complexity = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Tool": ["cityseer", "madina", "sDNA", "flownet", "aequilibrae"],
        "Integration LoC": [1436, 155, 225, 313, 339],
        "Tool source LoC": [8715, 3616, 17173, 1847, 16248],
    }
)
tbl_complexity["Total LoC"] = tbl_complexity["Integration LoC"] + tbl_complexity["Tool source LoC"]
tbl_complexity
```

## Reproducibility

The suite is designed to make every number in this paper regenerable:

- **DVC pipeline.** `dvc.yaml` defines one stage per benchmark (e.g. `bench_centrality`, `bench_cityseer_demand`, `bench_madina_gravity`, `bench_sdna`, `bench_flownet`, and the Leeds equivalents `bench_cityseer_od_leeds`, `bench_aequilibrae_leeds`), plus data preparation (`prepare_demand`, `prepare_leeds_ground_truth`, `generate_networks`, `generate_networks_leeds`), the `clip_leeds_inputs` side-effect stage, result merging (`merge_results`, `merge_results_leeds`) and report rendering (`render_report`). `dvc repro` from the repository root regenerates every stage; `dvc.lock` records the hashes of all inputs and outputs.
- **Docker image.** The multi-stage `Dockerfile` first builds the sDNA+ C++ library with OpenMP, then installs the Python/R toolchain on `ghcr.io/geocompx/python` (Python 3.12, Debian Bookworm) and runs `dvc repro` as the container command: `docker build -t cenbench . && docker run cenbench`.
- **Pinned versions.** cityseer `4.24.1`, aequilibrae `1.7.0`, flownet `0.3.0` (R package), madina (`fix-pandas-numpy-compat` branch), sDNA+ `4.1.1` (Cross_platform branch), pandas `>=3.0`, Quarto `1.8.27` (pinned in the Dockerfile) and R from the base image. `requirements.txt` pins the Python stack; the flownet runner is `scripts/run_flownet_assignment.R`.
- **Random seeds.** The OD sampling in `scripts/bench_cityseer_od.py` uses `np.random.RandomState(42)`; all other runners are deterministic given their inputs.
- **Ground truth regeneration.** Leeds AADT counts come from `scripts/prepare_leeds_ground_truth.py`; the census OD matrix and MSOA zones are fetched by `scripts/fetch_pct_od.R` via `pct::get_od` (MSOA geography). Leuven Telraam counts are fetched from the Telraam API.
- **The 10 km clip.** `scripts/clip_leeds_inputs.py` applies the circular 10 km buffer clip to the Leeds networks, DfT AADT points and PCT zones/OD pairs in place (a side-effect DVC stage), so the clipped inputs are exactly the ones benchmarked.
- **Efficiency score.** Defined in Equation @eq-efficiency; the merged result CSVs carry a precomputed `efficiency_score` column using the same formula.
- **Rendering this paper.** From the `paper/` directory, with the repository virtualenv active: `quarto render index.qmd --to html`. All tables and figures are computed at render time from `results/`, so re-rendering picks up any updated benchmark outputs.

# Results

All tables and figures in this section are computed live from `results/leuven_results.csv` and `results/leeds_results.csv` at render time, so they always reflect the current benchmark outputs.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: setup
# Imports and data loading — suppressed from the rendered paper.
import os

import pandas as pd

results_dir = os.path.join("..", "results")
leuven = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(results_dir, "leuven_results.csv"))
leeds = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(results_dir, "leeds_results.csv"))

# Normalise string columns (arrow-backed dtypes otherwise trip up masking).
for _df in (leuven, leeds):
    for _col in ("tool", "mode", "variant"):
        _df[_col] = _df[_col].astype(str)

# Map each result tool to its LoC family (see Methods, Table tbl-complexity).
_loC_family = {
    "cityseer": "cityseer",
    "cityseer_demand": "cityseer",
    "cityseer_od": "cityseer",
    "madina": "madina",
    "madina_worldpop": "madina",
    "sdna": "sDNA",
    "flownet": "flownet",
    "aequilibrae": "aequilibrae",
}
```

## Walking (Leuven, Telraam)

Table @tbl-leuven reports, for each tool, the best-performing variant by efficiency score on Leuven walk flows.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-leuven
#| tbl-cap: "Best variant per tool by efficiency score — Leuven, walk mode (Telraam ground truth). All eight tools have merged Leuven results. R² rows for cityseer_od and aequilibrae use log-log R²; all other rows use linear R², so values are not directly comparable across rows."
leuven_walk = leuven[leuven["mode"] == "walk"].copy()
tbl_leuven = (
    leuven_walk.sort_values("efficiency_score", ascending=False)
    .groupby("tool", as_index=False)
    .first()
    [["tool", "variant", "r_squared", "compute_time_s", "peak_memory_mb", "efficiency_score"]]
    .copy()
)
tbl_leuven.columns = ["Tool", "Best variant", "R²", "Time (s)", "Peak memory (MB)", "Efficiency score"]
tbl_leuven = tbl_leuven.sort_values("Efficiency score", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
tbl_leuven["R²"] = tbl_leuven["R²"].round(4)
tbl_leuven["Time (s)"] = tbl_leuven["Time (s)"].round(2)
tbl_leuven["Peak memory (MB)"] = tbl_leuven["Peak memory (MB)"].round(1)
tbl_leuven["Efficiency score"] = tbl_leuven["Efficiency score"].round(3)
tbl_leuven
```

Four findings stand out for walk flows:

- **Demand explains pedestrian counts; centrality does not.** The two gravity-demand models lead on accuracy: madina_worldpop (linear R² 0.876) and cityseer_demand (0.676), both sharing the same synthetic WorldPop × POI gravity demand. The pure centrality variants of cityseer, madina and flownet explain almost none of the variance in pedestrian counts (R² 0.004–0.145), and even the best centrality-only tool (sDNA+, 0.468) trails the demand-driven models.
- **The efficiency score reorders the ranking.** cityseer_od tops Table @tbl-leuven (efficiency 3.07) despite an R² of only 0.105 (log-log), because it runs in 0.03 s versus 48.3 s for madina_worldpop — a ~1,600× runtime advantage that the score's log-scale penalty rewards. Accuracy-only ranking would put madina_worldpop first.
- **Equilibrium helps on walk flows too.** aequilibrae's UE variants (log-log R² up to 0.155) beat its AoN baseline (0.084), though its BPR capacity model assumes vehicles and walk-mode results are therefore approximate (Limitations).
- **The evidence base is thin:** only 22 Telraam sensors matched the Leuven network, so all Leuven R² values are computed on a small sample.

## Driving (Leeds, DfT AADT)

Table @tbl-leeds reports the best variant per tool by efficiency score on Leeds drive flows, and Table @tbl-leeds-top3 zooms into the top three variants of the best tool (cityseer_od).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-leeds
#| tbl-cap: "Best variant per tool by efficiency score — Leeds, drive mode (DfT AADT ground truth). All seven tools are shown, sorted by efficiency score. R² rows for cityseer_od and aequilibrae use log-log R²; all other rows use linear R², so values are not directly comparable across rows. aequilibrae's row is its all-or-nothing variant, which wins on speed even though UE fits better (see text)."
leeds_drive = leeds[leeds["mode"] == "drive"].copy()
tbl_leeds = (
    leeds_drive.sort_values("efficiency_score", ascending=False)
    .groupby("tool", as_index=False)
    .first()
    [["tool", "variant", "r_squared", "compute_time_s", "peak_memory_mb", "efficiency_score"]]
    .copy()
)
tbl_leeds.columns = ["Tool", "Best variant", "R²", "Time (s)", "Peak memory (MB)", "Efficiency score"]
tbl_leeds = tbl_leeds.sort_values("Efficiency score", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
tbl_leeds["R²"] = tbl_leeds["R²"].round(4)
tbl_leeds["Time (s)"] = tbl_leeds["Time (s)"].round(2)
tbl_leeds["Peak memory (MB)"] = tbl_leeds["Peak memory (MB)"].round(1)
tbl_leeds["Efficiency score"] = tbl_leeds["Efficiency score"].round(3)
tbl_leeds
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-leeds-top3
#| tbl-cap: "Top three variants of the best-performing tool (cityseer_od) on Leeds drive flows, by efficiency score. All three use census OD demand with importance-weighted centroid dispersion."
best_tool = tbl_leeds.iloc[0]["Tool"]
tbl_top3 = (
    leeds_drive[leeds_drive["tool"] == best_tool]
    .sort_values("efficiency_score", ascending=False)
    .head(3)
    [["variant", "r_squared", "compute_time_s", "peak_memory_mb", "efficiency_score"]]
    .copy()
)
tbl_top3.columns = ["Variant", "R²", "Time (s)", "Peak memory (MB)", "Efficiency score"]
tbl_top3 = tbl_top3.reset_index(drop=True)
tbl_top3["R²"] = tbl_top3["R²"].round(4)
tbl_top3["Time (s)"] = tbl_top3["Time (s)"].round(2)
tbl_top3["Peak memory (MB)"] = tbl_top3["Peak memory (MB)"].round(1)
tbl_top3["Efficiency score"] = tbl_top3["Efficiency score"].round(3)
tbl_top3
```

Five findings stand out for drive flows:

- **Demand realism beats algorithm sophistication.** cityseer_od with the real census OD matrix reaches log-log R² 0.180 at 0.04 s per run — an order of magnitude better than the synthetic gravity demand (madina_worldpop, 0.022) on the same network. The gap between demand inputs (0.022 → 0.180) dwarfs any algorithm-level difference measured here (see below).
- **Dispersion beats tolerance, and both beat plain assignment.** The top three cityseer_od variants (Table @tbl-leeds-top3) all use importance-weighted *centroid* dispersion at 3% tolerance: R² 0.180 at a 5 km radius. Dispersion around the OD centroid outperforms zone-based k-dispersion (best k3/k5/k10 R² 0.073–0.107), and tolerance effects saturate in the 2–5% range (tol 0.03 ≈ tol 0.0 at fixed radius; tol 0.05 slightly worse).
- **User equilibrium beats all-or-nothing.** aequilibrae's UE (ue_bfw, log-log R² 0.096) beats its AoN baseline (0.083) — but AoN still wins inside aequilibrae by *efficiency* score, because UE costs ~1 s versus 0.12 s for roughly +0.01 R². This is exactly the accuracy–cost trade-off the efficiency score is designed to surface.
- **The 10 km clip leaves its fingerprint.** Zone-based k-dispersion reverses its full-region ranking inside the clip (Leeds k3 R² 0.073 < centroid 0.180), and cityseer_od's radius sweep (Figure @fig-dispersion) plateaus from 8–40 km — the clip bounds the reachable network, so larger radii add nothing.
- **flownet underperforms, and its PSL variants are not yet differentiated.** All six flownet beta/detour variants returned identical R² (0.0039, ~500 s each), because the runner does not yet vary the path-sized-logit hyperparameters; its potential is therefore untested by these results. sDNA+ reaches the best *linear* R² among the non-demand tools (0.123, MCF 200 m) but takes ~93 s and its fit is dominated by high-flow links; per-segment observed-vs-predicted plots are not yet shown because the prediction exports are not aligned with the benchmark metric path (Limitations).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-dispersion
#| fig-cap: "Radius sensitivity of cityseer_od on Leeds drive flows (census OD, centroid dispersion, 3% tolerance, log-log R²). Accuracy peaks at a 5 km radius (R² 0.180) and plateaus at ≈0.173 for radii of 8–40 km, consistent with the 10 km network clip bounding the reachable graph."
#| fig-format: png
#| fig-dpi: 150
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

_sweep = (
    leeds_drive[
        leeds_drive["tool"] == "cityseer_od"
    ]
    .copy()
)
_sweep["radius_m"] = _sweep["variant"].str.extract(r"_r(\d+)$").astype(float)
_sweep = _sweep[_sweep["variant"].str.contains("dimensionless_imp_centroid_tol0.03_")].sort_values("radius_m")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.6))
ax.semilogx(_sweep["radius_m"], _sweep["r_squared"], "o-", color="#1f77b4")
_peak = _sweep.loc[_sweep["r_squared"].idxmax()]
ax.annotate(
    f"peak R² {_peak['r_squared']:.3f}\nat 5 km",
    xy=(_peak["radius_m"], _peak["r_squared"]),
    xytext=(0.42, 0.62), textcoords="axes fraction",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="0.4"),
    fontsize=9,
)
ax.set_xlabel("Dispersion radius (m, log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Log-log R² (AADT)")
ax.set_title("cityseer_od radius sweep, Leeds drive", fontsize=10)
ax.axhline(0, color="0.8", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
fig.tight_layout()
```

## Cycling (coverage gap — no per-mode sensor data yet)

Cycle-flow estimates are conspicuously absent from the tables above, and the reason is data, not tooling. Both cities' cycle networks are already generated (`data/leuven_cycle_edges.gpkg`, `data/leeds_cycle_edges.gpkg`, produced by the `generate_networks` stages) and every tool in the suite can run on them, but no per-mode cycle ground truth has been integrated yet: Telraam's Leuven sensors are used for pedestrians, DfT's AADT points for Leeds traffic, and neither provides matched cycle counts in the current data. Closing this gap is a priority — Telraam cycle counts and DfT cycle flow data are both candidate ground truths — and the suite needs only a sensors file and a `config/cities.yaml` entry to add the mode.

## Efficiency frontier

Figure @fig-efficiency plots every benchmarked variant — one point per variant — with runtime on a log x-axis and R² on the y-axis, for Leeds drive (left) and Leuven walk (right). The Pareto frontier of *fast and accurate* sits in the top-left: cityseer_od occupies it on both cities, combining the best fit with millisecond runtimes, while flownet anchors the opposite corner (~500 s for R² 0.004). The efficiency score is the single-number summary of this frontier: it ranks cityseer_od first in both cities precisely because it is the only tool that is both accurate and cheap.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-efficiency
#| fig-cap: "Efficiency frontier: runtime (log x-axis) versus R² for every benchmarked variant, coloured by tool. Left: Leeds drive (log-log R² for cityseer_od and aequilibrae, linear R² otherwise). Right: Leuven walk (same metric split). Best-per-tool variants are labelled. The Pareto frontier of fast + accurate sits top-left; cityseer_od occupies it on both cities, flownet the bottom-right."
#| fig-format: png
#| fig-dpi: 150
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
#| warning: false

_tools_all = sorted(set(leeds["tool"]) | set(leuven["tool"]))
_cmap = {t: plt.cm.tab10(i % 10) for i, t in enumerate(_tools_all)}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.4))
for ax, (title, df) in zip(
    axes,
    [("Leeds drive (DfT AADT)", leeds_drive), ("Leuven walk (Telraam)", leuven_walk)],
):
    for tool, grp in df.groupby("tool"):
        ax.scatter(
            grp["compute_time_s"], grp["r_squared"],
            s=22, alpha=0.75, color=_cmap[tool],
            edgecolors="none", label=tool,
        )
    _best = (
        df.sort_values("efficiency_score", ascending=False)
        .groupby("tool", as_index=False)
        .first()
    )
    _off = {
        "cityseer_od": (8, 6), "aequilibrae": (8, -14), "sdna": (8, 2),
        "cityseer": (8, -4), "madina": (8, 4), "madina_worldpop": (8, 6),
        "flownet": (8, -2), "cityseer_demand": (8, 4),
    }
    for _, row in _best.iterrows():
        _dx, _dy = _off.get(row["tool"], (6, 6))
        ax.annotate(
            row["tool"], xy=(row["compute_time_s"], row["r_squared"]),
            xytext=(_dx, _dy), textcoords="offset points",
            fontsize=7.5, color=_cmap[row["tool"]],
        )
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel("Compute time (s, log scale)")
    ax.set_ylabel("R²")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.8", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
    ax.text(
        0.03, 0.97, "fast + accurate\n(Pareto frontier)", transform=ax.transAxes,
        va="top", fontsize=8, color="0.35",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc="white", ec="0.8", lw=0.8),
    )
fig.tight_layout()
```

## Accuracy versus complexity

Figure @fig-complexity places each tool family by its source-code size (log x-axis) and the best R² it achieves on Leeds drive flows, coloured by the efficiency score of that best variant. The headline: the cityseer family — 8.7k lines of Python (Rust core excluded) plus a ~1.4k-line integration, including a small OD-assignment script — delivers the best fit (log-log R² 0.180) at 0.04 s, while aequilibrae's 16.2k-line codebase reaches 0.096 at ~1 s and sDNA+'s 17.2k-line C++ reaches linear R² 0.123 at ~93 s. flownet's 1.8k lines are the cheapest to read but the most expensive to run (~500 s) for the weakest fit. Efficiency — accuracy per unit of compute — correlates with *small* codebases here, not large ones.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-complexity
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy versus complexity on Leeds drive flows: tool source LoC (log x-axis) versus the best R² achieved by that tool family (max over variants), labelled by the best-performing member. Open markers: log-log R² (cityseer_od, aequilibrae); filled: linear R². Colour: efficiency score of the labelled variant. cityseer's Rust core and aequilibrae's C++ core are excluded from the Python LoC counts."
#| fig-format: png
#| fig-dpi: 150
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
#| warning: false

_loC = tbl_complexity.set_index("Tool")["Tool source LoC"].to_dict()
_fam_rows = []
for _fam_name, _fam_grp in leeds_drive.groupby(leeds_drive["tool"].map(_loC_family)):
    _best_row = _fam_grp.sort_values("r_squared", ascending=False).iloc[0]
    _fam_rows.append(
        {
            "family": _fam_name,
            "best_tool": _best_row["tool"],
            "r_squared": _best_row["r_squared"],
            "efficiency_score": _best_row["efficiency_score"],
            "compute_time_s": _best_row["compute_time_s"],
        }
    )
_fam = pd.DataFrame(_fam_rows).reset_index(drop=True)
_fam["source_LoC"] = _fam["family"].map(_loC)
_fam = _fam.sort_values("source_LoC")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.6))
_sc = ax.scatter(
    _fam["source_LoC"], _fam["r_squared"],
    c=_fam["efficiency_score"], cmap="viridis", norm=plt.matplotlib.colors.LogNorm(),
    s=90, zorder=3,
)
for _, row in _fam.iterrows():
    _open = row["best_tool"] in ("cityseer_od", "aequilibrae")
    ax.scatter(
        row["source_LoC"], row["r_squared"],
        facecolor="none" if _open else _sc.cmap(_sc.norm(row["efficiency_score"])),
        edgecolors="k", s=90, zorder=4, lw=1.0,
    )
    ax.annotate(
        f"{row['best_tool']}\n(R² {row['r_squared']:.3f}, {row['compute_time_s']:.1f}s)",
        xy=(row["source_LoC"], row["r_squared"]),
        xytext=(8, 5), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8,
    )
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Tool source LoC (log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Best R², Leeds drive")
ax.axhline(0, color="0.8", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
_cbar = fig.colorbar(_sc, ax=ax)
_cbar.set_label("Efficiency score of best variant", fontsize=8)
_cbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
fig.tight_layout()
```

# Discussion

**Q1 — The route-choice model class matters, but modestly.** On Leeds drive flows, dispersed and equilibrium assignment consistently beat the AoN baseline: aequilibrae UE (log-log R² 0.096) beats AoN (0.083), and cityseer_od's dispersed centroid assignment (0.180) beats its plain shortest-path variant (0.074). Dispersion around the OD centroid matters more than the tolerance setting, which saturates in the 2–5% range. But the most sophisticated class in the suite — flownet's path-sized logit — shows no signal yet: all six variants returned identical predictions (a runner limitation, not evidence against PSL), so the ceiling of the model-class ladder remains untested.

**Q2 — Demand realism dominates algorithm sophistication.** The single largest effect in the benchmark is the demand input. On Leeds, replacing synthetic gravity demand with the real census OD matrix moves log-log R² from 0.022 (madina_worldpop) to 0.180 (cityseer_od) — an eightfold improvement — while the largest algorithm-level effect measured (UE vs AoN) moves R² by only ~0.01. On Leuven walk flows, the pattern inverts in spirit: the gravity demand model explains most of the variance (linear R² 0.68–0.88) because pedestrian counts around Leuven are well predicted by population and POI attractors, and pure centrality explains almost nothing. Demand realism matters most where demand drives the model — and it matters more than the assignment algorithm everywhere.

**Q3 — The efficiency score changes the rankings.** An accuracy-only ranking would lead with madina_worldpop on Leuven (R² 0.876) and cityseer_od on Leeds (0.180). The efficiency score reorders both cities: cityseer_od wins Leuven too (3.07 vs 0.21 for madina_worldpop, a ~1,600× runtime gap), and inside aequilibrae the AoN variant outranks UE despite fitting worse, because UE buys +0.01 R² at ~10× the runtime. flownet drops to last place everywhere: ~500 s per run for R² 0.004. The frontier figure (Figure @fig-efficiency) makes the trade-off visible: the top-left corner belongs to tools that are both accurate and cheap, which is the combination that matters for city-scale application.

**Complexity-adjusted comparison.** The complexity figure (Figure @fig-complexity) tempers the headline ranking. Aequilibrae's 16.2k lines of source deliver roughly +0.01 R² over the cityseer family's 8.7k lines at the assignment level, and cityseer's Rust core is deliberately excluded from its Python LoC — so apparent differences in code size overstate differences in engineering effort. Whether the extra machinery is worthwhile depends on the application: production traffic models need aequilibrae's equilibrium and matrix tools; rapid screening may not.

**Mode coverage.** Results are limited to walk (Leuven) and drive (Leeds); cycle flows await sensor data, with the networks and tooling already in place (Results — Cycling). Rankings are mode-dependent: madina_worldpop leads accuracy on Leuven walk but sits near the bottom on Leeds drive, which is exactly why per-mode benchmarking matters.

# Limitations

- **R² metric mismatch across cities and tools**: linear R² is used for Leuven Telraam walk counts and for all centrality/gravity tools, while log-log R² is used for Leeds AADT and for the cityseer_od and aequilibrae rows in both tables; R² values are therefore not directly comparable across rows, tables or cities. The metrics helpers (`compute_metrics` vs `compute_metrics_loglog`) should report both scales in future runs.
- **Single city per mode so far**: walk is only benchmarked in Leuven and drive only in Leeds, so tool rankings may not generalise across urban contexts.
- **Leeds clip boundary artefact**: the 10 km buffer clip around central Leeds breaks zone-based k-dispersion, reversing the k3 vs centroid ranking seen on the full region, and caps the effective dispersion radius at the clip extent (Figure @fig-dispersion).
- **flownet is not yet exercised**: its demand is synthetic everywhere, and its PSL beta/detour hyperparameters were not varied by the runner, so all six variants returned identical predictions; the path-sized-logit model class is consequently untested by these results.
- **Demand and mode approximations**: aequilibrae's walk-mode assignment is an approximation (the BPR capacity model assumes vehicles; the AoN baseline is unaffected).
- **Small sensor samples**: 22 matched Telraam sensors in Leuven and 181–197 matched AADT links in Leeds (where recorded) bound the statistical power of every R² here.
- **Per-segment prediction exports are not yet aligned with the benchmark metric path**: the `results/*_best_predictions.csv` files are produced by different code paths (interactive-map and sDNA+ runners) than the metrics in the result tables and are stale relative to the current results, so observed-vs-predicted plots are omitted from this paper until the export paths are aligned with the `compute_metrics` pipeline.

# Conclusion

These results invite extension rather than conclusion. The three questions answered here — route-choice model class matters modestly, demand realism dominates algorithm choice, and the efficiency score reorders the ranking — each deserve more cities, more modes and more tools. Oxford is a candidate city, cycle counts are the obvious missing mode (the networks and tooling are ready), and flownet's PSL class needs a runner that varies its hyperparameters before its model class can be judged. The suite is designed to make this cheap: a new city needs a `config/cities.yaml` entry, ground-truth and demand preparation scripts, and a per-tool runner — contributions to the cenbench repository are welcome.
